intro: Four modules cover the practical Docker skills an IT professional needs: containers and images, running and inspecting containers, building images, and Compose with networking and housekeeping. Practice in the labs and use the Reference tab as a cheat sheet.

modules.title: Containers, images and registries
modules.summary: Understand what a container is, how it differs from a virtual machine, and how images and registries fit together.

blocks.p: A container is a normal process on a host that is isolated from other processes and given its own view of the file system, network and users. It carries the application and everything it needs (libraries, runtime) so it runs the same on a laptop, a server or the cloud. Containers share the host's operating system kernel, which makes them small and fast to start.

head: Container
Virtual machine
rows: Full OS with its own kernel

blocks.p: An image is a read-only template made of layers: base operating system files, then your app. A container is a running (or stopped) instance of an image, with a thin writable layer on top. One image can start many containers.

blocks.note: Image = recipe and ingredients. Container = the meal being cooked. Delete the container and the image is untouched.

blocks.p: A registry stores images. Docker Hub is the default public one; companies often run private registries (Azure Container Registry, Amazon ECR, GitHub Container Registry). An image name looks like registry/namespace/name:tag, for example nginx:1.27. If you leave off the tag you get latest, which is a moving target, so pin a version for anything important.

tips: Containers are not tiny VMs: they share the host kernel.
Pin image tags (nginx:1.27) instead of relying on latest.
Only pull images from sources you trust; images can contain malware or outdated software.
terms: An isolated running process created from an image.
A read-only, layered template used to create containers.
A service that stores and distributes images, such as Docker Hub.
A label for an image version, like 1.27 or latest.
Software that builds and runs containers, such as Docker or Podman.
One step of an image; layers are cached and shared.

slides.title: What a container is
bullets: Packages the app and its libraries
script: A container is an isolated process that carries everything the application needs. It shares the host's kernel, so it is light and fast.

slides.title: Containers versus VMs
script: Virtual machines each carry an operating system. Containers share one kernel, so they are smaller and start faster.

slides.title: Image to container
script: You build or pull an image, then start one or many containers from it.

slides.title: Names and tags
script: Image names include a tag. Latest can change at any time, so pin a version for repeatable results.

modules.title: Running and managing containers
modules.summary: Start containers, publish ports, set environment variables, persist data with volumes and inspect what is running.

cmds: Run a container from an image (pulls it if needed)
Run in the background, name it, map host port 8080 to container port 80
Interactive shell inside a new container
Delete the container when it exits
head: Command
What it does

blocks.note: -p HOST:CONTAINER: the first number is the port on your machine, the second is inside the container. -p 8080:80 means browse to http://localhost:8080.

cmds: Open a shell in a running container
docker stop web / docker start web
head: Command
What it does

blocks.p: Pass configuration with environment variables: -e DB_HOST=db.example.com. A container's writable layer disappears when the container is removed, so keep data you care about in a volume (-v dbdata:/var/lib/mysql) or a bind mount (-v /srv/site:/usr/share/nginx/html).

blocks.note: Never put passwords in an image or commit them to Git. Pass secrets at run time or use a secrets manager.

tips: docker ps -a shows stopped containers too: use it when something "disappeared".
Use docker logs first when a container exits immediately.
Use --rm for throwaway test containers so they do not pile up.
terms: -p host:container: forwards a host port into a container.
A host folder mounted into a container.
Run a command inside a running container.
A setting passed to the container, -e NAME=value.

slides.title: Start a container
script: Docker run creates a container from an image and starts it. Add detached to run it in the background.

slides.title: Publish a port
script: The port option forwards a port on your machine to a port in the container.

slides.title: Inspect and troubleshoot
script: Use ps to see what is running, logs to read output and exec to look inside.

visual.text:
docker ps -a
docker logs web
docker exec -it web sh

slides.title: Keep your data
script: The writable layer disappears with the container. Use volumes for data and pass secrets at run time.

modules.title: Building images with a Dockerfile
modules.summary: Write a simple Dockerfile, build and tag an image, and understand layers and caching.

blocks.p: A Dockerfile is a text recipe that builds an image, one instruction per layer.

cmds: Copy a file from your project into the image
Run a command at build time
Copy the rest of the code
Document the port the app listens on
The default command when a container starts
head: Instruction
What it does

cmds: Build an image from the Dockerfile in this folder
head: Command
What it does

blocks.p: Each instruction creates a layer and Docker caches layers that did not change. Put things that change rarely (installing dependencies) before things that change often (your source code) so rebuilds are fast. Smaller images start faster and have fewer vulnerabilities.

list: Use a slim or minimal base image
Add a .dockerignore file to keep .git, logs and secrets out of the build
Run as a non-root user (USER app)
Use multi-stage builds so build tools are not in the final image

tips: Order matters: copy dependency files first, install, then copy the code.
CMD is the default command; RUN happens at build time only.
Scan images for known vulnerabilities before you ship them.
terms: Text file of instructions for building an image.
The folder of files sent to Docker during docker build.
Reuse of unchanged layers to speed up builds.
What runs when a container starts.
Using one stage to build and another, smaller one to run.
Lists files to exclude from the build context.

slides.title: Dockerfile basics
script: A Dockerfile lists steps that build your image. Each step is a layer.

visual.text:
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "app.py"]

slides.title: Build and tag
bullets: The dot is the build context
script: Run docker build in the folder with the Dockerfile and give the image a name and tag.

visual.text:
docker build -t myapp:1.0 .
docker run -d -p 8000:8000 myapp:1.0

slides.title: Use the cache
script: Docker reuses unchanged layers. Install dependencies before copying the code that changes often.

slides.title: Smaller and safer
script: Keep images small, run as a non-root user and keep secrets out of the build.

modules.title: Compose, networking and housekeeping
modules.summary: Run multi-container apps with Compose, understand container networking and keep a Docker host tidy and secure.

blocks.p: Compose describes a multi-container application in one YAML file, usually compose.yaml, and starts everything with one command.

cmds: Create and start all services in the background
Stop and remove them (add -v to remove volumes too)
head: Command
What it does

blocks.note: A service can reach another by its service name, for example db:5432, because Compose creates a network with built-in name resolution.

head: Network type
What it does
rows: Private network on the host; containers talk to each other and use NAT to reach out
Container shares the host's network stack
Containers resolve each other by name

blocks.p: Only published ports (-p) are reachable from outside the host. Everything else stays private.

cmds: Remove stopped containers, unused networks and dangling images
head: Command
What it does

list: Keep the host and images patched
Do not run containers with --privileged unless you must
Never expose the Docker socket (/var/run/docker.sock) to containers or the network: it gives root-level control

tips: Compose is for development and small deployments; production fleets usually use an orchestrator such as Kubernetes.
docker compose down -v deletes volumes and their data.
Read the Compose file first: it documents every service, port and volume.
terms: A tool and file format for running multi-container apps.
One container definition in a Compose file.
The default private network for containers on a host.
Delete unused Docker objects to free space.
The API endpoint that controls Docker; treat it like root access.
Software such as Kubernetes that schedules containers across many hosts.

slides.title: Compose in one file
bullets: One YAML file for the app
script: Compose lets you define a web app and a database together and start both with one command.

visual.text:
services:
  web:
    image: nginx:1.27
    ports: ["8080:80"]
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    volumes: ["dbdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data"]
volumes:
  dbdata:

slides.title: Container networking
script: Containers on a bridge network can talk to each other. Only published ports are reachable from outside.

slides.title: Keep it tidy
script: Docker can use a lot of disk. Check usage and prune carefully.

visual.text:
docker system df
docker system prune
docker stats

slides.title: Security basics
script: Treat access to the Docker socket like root access, and avoid giving containers more privilege than they need.
